problem: Rochester asks Jane to say the words 'Edward, I will marry you', but without inner quotation marks it reads (and sounds) as if he himself says 'I will marry you'.
new_text: "Gratitude!" he exclaimed, and added wildly—"Jane, accept me quickly. Say, 'Edward'—give me my name—'Edward, I will marry you.'"

problem: 'The moon had not yet set, and we were all in shadow' reads as a contradiction; the point is that clouds have covered the still-risen moon.
new_text: But what had happened to the night? The moon had not yet set, yet we were all in shadow; I could barely see my master's face, near as I was. And what was wrong with the chestnut tree? It writhed and groaned; while wind roared through the laurel walk and swept over us.

problem: 'a beauty just after the desire of my heart' uses archaic 'after' (= according to); a modern reader will not parse it.
new_text: "You are a beauty in my eyes, and a beauty exactly as my heart desires — delicate and ethereal."

problem: The second clause ('for I take that comforting belief to heart, Jane, a faith in your affection') is tangled; the appositive dangles.
new_text: "That you may, my good little girl. There is not another being in the world who has the same pure love for me as yourself — and I hold that comforting belief close to my heart, Jane: faith in your affection."

problem: Final sentence mixes direct and reported speech inside one quotation: '"It will do for the present," he said, "but he would yet see me glittering..."' — 'he' and 'me' inside the quote make no sense as Rochester's own words.
new_text: The hour spent at Millcote was somewhat trying for me. Mr. Rochester made me go to a certain silk warehouse, where I was ordered to choose half a dozen dresses. I hated the business and begged to put it off — but no, it had to be done now. By means of urgent whispers, I reduced the half dozen to two. These, however, he vowed he would select himself. With anxiety I watched his eye roam over the colourful displays. He settled on a rich silk of the most brilliant amethyst and a superb pink satin. I told him in a fresh series of whispers that he might as well buy me a gold gown and a silver bonnet at once — I would certainly never dare to wear his choices. With enormous difficulty, for he was stubborn as a stone, I persuaded him to exchange them for a sober black satin and a pearl-grey silk. "It will do for the present," he said; but he would yet see me glittering like a flower garden.

problem: 'a second Danaë with the golden shower falling daily around me' — the myth is obscure to most readers, and 'golden shower' on its own carries an unintended modern meaning that could jar, especially read aloud. A brief gloss keeps the image clear.
new_text: I was glad to get him out of the silk warehouse, and then out of a jeweller's shop. The more he bought me, the more my cheeks burned with annoyance and humiliation. As we got back into the carriage and I sat back, flushed and worn out, I remembered what, in the rush of events, dark and bright, I had completely forgotten — the letter from my uncle, John Eyre, to Mrs. Reed, about his intention to adopt me and make me his heir. "It would, indeed, be a relief," I thought, "if I had even the smallest independence. I can never bear being dressed like a doll by Mr. Rochester, or sitting like a second Danaë — the princess of the old myth whom Jupiter visited as a rain of gold — with gold raining daily around me. I will write to Madeira the moment I get home and tell my uncle John I am going to be married, and to whom. If I had even the prospect of one day bringing Mr. Rochester an addition to his fortune, I could better endure being kept by him now." Somewhat comforted by this idea (which I carried out that very day), I ventured once more to meet my master's and lover's eye, which persistently sought mine, though I had been avoiding both his face and his gaze. He smiled, and I thought his smile was the kind a sultan might bestow, in a happy, fond moment, on a slave his gold and gems had enriched. I crushed his hand — which was forever chasing mine — vigorously, and thrust it back to him red from the passionate pressure.

problem: From 24.151 to 24.178 both speakers' lines are given as reported speech inside quotation marks ('his darling Jane', 'Did I like his voice?'). With no speaker tags a reader or listener loses track of who is talking. Adding a tag on Rochester's untagged lines fixes it without changing the device.
new_text: "That was a strange question to be put by his darling Jane," he said.

problem: Same reported-speech passage: Rochester's line uses 'he' for himself and 'I' for Jane, and has no speaker tag. It reads as if Jane is speaking.
new_text: "Oh, all he longed, all he prayed for, was that I might live with him!" he protested. "Death was not for such as I."

problem: Same reported-speech passage: this untagged line is Rochester's, but it follows Jane's line directly.
new_text: "Would I forgive him for the selfish idea and prove my pardon by a reconciling kiss?" he asked.

problem: Same reported-speech passage: this untagged line is Rochester's, but it follows Jane's narration directly.
new_text: "Would I be quiet and talk rationally?" he asked.

problem: The final clause is tangled: 'while feeding his tyranny more, would have pleased his judgment... and even suited his taste less'. The word 'less' comes only at the very end, so on first hearing the sentence seems to say the opposite of what it means.
new_text: The system I had started, I pursued throughout the whole trial period, and with great success. He was kept, to be sure, rather cross and grumpy. But on the whole I could see he was excellently entertained, and that a lamb-like submission and dove-like tenderness would have fed his tyranny more, but would have pleased his judgment less, satisfied his common sense less, and even suited his taste less.

problem: 'the filmy veil hanging from the claimed trunk' — the meaning of 'claimed' is unclear. The sense is that the trunk has been taken over by the not-yet-existing Mrs. Rochester.
new_text: The month of courtship had run its course. Its very last hours were being counted down. There was no putting off the day that was coming — the wedding day — and all preparations for its arrival were complete. I, at least, had nothing more to do. There were my trunks, packed, locked, corded, lined up in a row along the wall of my little room. Tomorrow, at this time, they would be far along the road to London, and so would I (God willing) — or rather, not I, but one Jane Rochester, a person I did not yet know. The address cards alone remained to be attached. They lay, four little squares, in the drawer. Mr. Rochester had himself written the direction, "Mrs. Rochester, —— Hotel, London," on each. I could not bring myself to attach them, or to have them attached. Mrs. Rochester! She did not exist. She would not be born until tomorrow, sometime after eight o'clock in the morning. I would wait to be assured she had come into the world alive before I assigned to her all that property. It was enough that in the closet opposite my dressing table, garments said to be hers had already displaced my black Lowood dress and straw bonnet. For that suit of wedding clothes did not belong to me — the pearl-coloured gown, the filmy veil hanging from the trunk she had taken over. I shut the closet to conceal the strange, ghost-like clothing it contained, which, at this evening hour — nine o'clock — certainly gave off a most eerie shimmer through the shadows of my room. "I will leave you by yourself, white dream," I said. "I am feverish. I hear the wind blowing. I will go outdoors and feel it."

problem: Jane's action ('I shook my head.') and Rochester's reply share one paragraph with no speaker tag, so it reads as if Jane says 'What! Is there more?'.
new_text: I shook my head. "What!" he said. "Is there more? But I will not believe it to be anything important. I warn you of my disbelief beforehand. Go on."

problem: 'the Funchal correspondent of his firm' — here 'correspondent' is an old trade term for a business agent. A modern reader will take it to mean a journalist or someone who writes letters.
new_text: "Mr. Mason does. Mr. Eyre has been the Funchal agent of his firm for some years. When your uncle received your letter mentioning the planned union between yourself and Mr. Rochester, Mr. Mason, who was staying in Madeira to restore his health on his way back to Jamaica, happened to be with him. Mr. Eyre mentioned the news, for he knew that my client here was acquainted with a gentleman named Rochester. Mr. Mason, as astonished and distressed as you may imagine, revealed the true state of affairs. Your uncle, I am sorry to say, is now on his sickbed — from which, considering the nature of his disease — a wasting decline — and the stage it has reached, it is unlikely he will ever rise. He could not then hurry to England himself to rescue you from the trap you had fallen into, but he begged Mr. Mason to lose no time in taking steps to prevent the fraudulent marriage. He referred him to me for help. I acted with all speed, and am thankful I was not too late — as you, no doubt, must be also. Were I not morally certain that your uncle will be dead before you reach Madeira, I would advise you to accompany Mr. Mason back. But as it is, I think you had better remain in England until you can hear further, either from or of Mr. Eyre. Have we anything else to stay for?" he asked of Mr. Mason.
